questions.q: How was the world connected in the pre-modern and nineteenth-century periods?

answer.text: The world has long been connected through trade and migration. The Silk Routes linked Asia with Europe and North Africa, carrying silk, spices and precious metals, as well as ideas and religions. After Columbus reached the Americas, foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chillies spread to the rest of the world, while diseases like smallpox devastated the native peoples of America.

In the nineteenth century the world economy was tied together by three flows — trade in goods, the movement of labour, and the flow of capital or investment. Cheap food imports followed the abolition of Britain's Corn Laws, and indentured labourers from India, called girmitiyas, were sent to plantations across the world in what became a new system of slavery.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Bretton Woods Conference?
answer: The Bretton Woods Conference, held in 1944 near the end of the Second World War, was called to build a stable framework for the post-war world economy.

answer.text: It set up two important institutions. The International Monetary Fund, or IMF, was created to deal with problems of balance of payments and to keep the international monetary system stable. The World Bank, formally the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, was set up to finance post-war reconstruction and later development.

The Bretton Woods system ushered in an era of remarkable growth in world trade and incomes for the Western industrial nations, and it still shapes the global economy today, even as decolonisation and the rise of newly independent nations transformed the world.
